papers.title: ARTICLE: Sovereign Debt Reform and the Best Interest of Creditors
papers.authors: William W. Bratton*, G. Mitu Gulati
papers.abstract:
This Article is about boilerplate language located at the back of contracts drafted by the world's largest law firms. The clauses in question are process provisions that regulate the amendment of sovereign debt contracts. These paragraphs have been drafted and redrafted by generations of corporate lawyers, yet they have changed little in their broad outlines in more than a century of use. Now they take center stage in the global financial arena, where they govern billions of dollars (and pounds, euros, and yen) of sovereign debt in default and billions more in imminent risk of default. Officials, academics, and even some of the lawyers who drafted the clauses now want the clauses removed because they make defaulted debt difficult to restructure.
How did this arcane preserve of the bond lawyer come to be the cutting edge in the evolution of international financial architecture? Whereas private debt defaults lead to bankruptcy, sovereign debt defaults lead to informal, often lengthy standstills. The creditors can wait out the period of distress, expecting eventual economic recovery to lead to a resumption of payments. But, for the most part, payment resumption requires that creditors come to the negotiating table to rewrite the defaulted debt contracts. Such a "composition" or "restructuring" scales down the sovereign's obligations and causes it to return to health quickly. In theory, this makes both the sovereign and its creditors better off.
There are practical barriers to be overcome before a composition can be concluded. These stem from information asymmetries, from coordination problems, or from complex bargaining dynamics. Sovereign compositions tend to be tripartite negotiations. In addition to the sovereign and the existing creditors, international financial institutions like the International Monetary Fund (IMF) come to the table holding out new loans. In theory, these loans are conditional, requiring the sovereign to reform its economic policies and the unpaid creditors to share the pain by cutting back their claims to induce lending that facilitates economic recovery. In practice, the IMF often acts precipitously, bailing out the sovereign so as to stabilize the international financial system or satisfy some other political goal of its major shareholders. The prospect of a bailout diminishes the creditors' incentive to come to the bargaining table to make concessions.
Assuming bargaining commences, the bond contracts contain boilerplate clauses, called "unanimous action clauses" (or "UACs"), that erect a barrier to success. These clauses, which conditionamendment of the bond contracts' key payment terms on unanimous bondholder consent, govern the majority of sovereign bonds outstanding. A minority of bond contracts contain "collective action clauses" (or "CACs"), which permit across-the-board amendments with a three-quarters majority. Whereas CACs facilitate restructuring of the defaulting sovereign's debt, UACs stand in the way. With thousands of bondholders dispersed around the globe, coordinating a unanimous vote is difficult, if not impossible. Further, a unanimous vote requirement invites free riding: Because the transaction makes the group as a whole better off, an opportunistic bondholder has an incentive to "hold out" - to withhold its essential vote in hopes of procuring a side payment from the transaction's proponents.
The cumulation of frictions has led to calls for the institution of a sovereign bankruptcy regime. This would resemble corporate bankruptcy reorganization, albeit tailored for sovereign debt. The IMF has proposed a minimal bankruptcy architecture, one that would trump UACs and facilitate restructuring in a majority action framework. The United States Treasury agreed on the need for majority action, but has registered a contractarian objection to the IMF's plan for a new statutory scheme: Since UACs lie at the core of the problem and UACs are contract terms, the solution lies in persuading the market to rewrite sovereign bond contracts rather than in overriding them with an international mandate. Now that the official sector refuses to bail out every sovereign in distress, Argentina being the most prominent example, UACs constitute less of a strategic advantage. On the assumption that CACs are otherwise superior to UACs in terms of efficiency, the Treasury projects that sovereign bondholders will willingly exchange their UAC bonds for CAC bonds, ameliorating the coordination problems. Sovereign debt restructuring can then go forward in a framework of free contract.
Sovereign bondholders and sovereign borrowers at first rejected both proposals - the IMF's bankruptcy plan and the Treasury's spontaneous bond exchange suggestion. These real parties in interest preferred the status quo. But their motives were suspect. To the extent that the status quo makes unconditional IMF bailouts more likely, the sovereigns and their lenders have reason to oppose reform, whether mandatory or contractual.Official sector pressurehas since broken the pattern of universal market opposition. A handful of sovereign issuers have successfully departed from market practice and include CACs in new bonds. The present question is whether this development heralds a market-wide shift to CACs as advocated by the Treasury.
This Article inquires into the causes of this multiparty dispute. It takes a new look at the economics of sovereign lending, identifying interests fundamental to the sovereign debtor-creditor relationship that have been obscured in a debate focused largely on opportunism occasioned by IMF bailout lending. This different focus leads us to identify unsound premises on both sides of the dispute between contract and mandate.
The contractarians propound a "free lunch" theory of sovereign lending. They assume that CACs are a first best improvement over UACs, and that a transition to CACs holds out a surplus for all parties to share. Unfortunately, no such twenty-dollar bill has been left lying on the table. In our view, sovereign lenders rationally could prefer UACs to CACs, and could do so even in a world without IMF bailout lending. It follows, on a worst-case scenario, that engrained resistance will prevent a voluntary, market-wide transition to CAC bonds, and that a majority action regime may be achieved only on a mandatory basis. On a best-case scenario, it follows that frictions will impede a market transition from UACs to CACs. If the international financial community wishes the incipient transition to become general and remain stable, it will have to pay for it. Yet it is unclear where the money would come from to pay UAC bondholders to trade their bonds for CAC bonds. In the alternative, the IMF will have to intervene aggressively, forcing model contract terms on sovereign borrowers by threatening penalties for those who borrow with UACs. The best-case scenario, thus characterized, is essentially mandatory intervention.
We accordingly agree with sovereign bankruptcy proponents who doubt that the markets will spontaneously and quickly shift from UACs to CACs once participants realize that bailouts are no longer readily available. But we also suggest that the bondholder community and the sovereign debtors have legitimate reasons for remaining suspicious of bankruptcy proposals. The IMF's proposal rests on a triad of majority action, cost savings, and administrative convenience as it simultaneously attempts to address the need for a better framework for bailout lending and to rationalize the process ofsovereign debt composition. These elements do not import a persuasive normative grounding for a bankruptcy regime. The economics of sovereign lending suggest a stronger, contract-based norm - the best interest of creditors,defined as whatever the unpaid lenders freely approve. Under the norm, only the creditors themselves should determine whether a given composition serves their best interests. It follows that a sovereign bankruptcy process should not attempt to replicate the transactional bias of American corporate reorganization, where the need to close the deal can override other concerns. In the sovereign context, the long-run interests of defaulting sovereigns and their creditors are more closely aligned than those of defaulting private borrowers and creditors. If sovereign creditors do not like the restructuring on offer, it must be allowed to fail.
Under this view, a sovereign bankruptcy regime need do little more than trump UACs with CACs and then leave the parties to renegotiate their contracts. With CACs in place (however imposed), the parties can be remitted to the law governing their contracts - the law of the State of New York in most cases - without needing the assistance of a bankruptcy infrastructure.
But one problem remains with this minimal approach, a problem stemming from the contractual jurisprudence of sovereign debt.Once a renegotiation framework is established, a given creditor's worst enemy may be neither the defaulting sovereign nor the IMF, but another creditor or group of creditors with conflicting interests. The contract law of New York is undeveloped on the question of whether sovereign creditors owe one another meaningful good faith duties. The law of private debtor-creditor relations, meanwhile, rejects the suggestion that creditors should owe duties to one another, leaving the job of constraining opportunistic behavior within the creditor group to the bankruptcy system.Over a century ago, however, in the period antedating the federal statutory reorganization regime, intercreditor duties did exist. As we see it, thematter of intercreditor equity became cabined in the federal bankruptcy reorganization regime after that regime appeared in 1934. Thereafter, state case law on intercreditor equity atrophied, replaced by a regime of contractual self-protection. A viable framework for sovereign restructuring, whether contract based or encapsulated in a bankruptcy regime, needs an adjudicatory authority willing to impose good faith duties across groups of creditors.
The Article proceeds as follows. Part II draws on the economics and practice of sovereign lending to assert that sovereign bankruptcy proposals should not be driven exclusively by the bailout problem. Reform proposals need to address the fundamentals of sovereign debtor-creditor relationships that operate independently of IMF intervention. These fundamentals help to articulate a contract-based norm, the best interest of creditors.
Part III looks at the sovereign bankruptcy movement to show that the best interest norm already has influenced its participants, albeit implicitly. The most prominent proposal, that of the IMF, has evolved towards both minimalism and creditor involvement. Some of what the IMF proposes to provide, however, is either unnecessary or inimical to the creditors' best interests. Most importantly, it is unclear that the IMF's involvement in the administration of such a system adds anything of value to either the sovereigns or their creditors.
Part IV appraises the CAC versus UAC debate. Here we encounter a puzzle: the persistent use for more than a century of UACs in New York-based sovereign debt issues and CACs in London-based debt issues. A frequent explanation of this puzzle centers on the Trust Indenture Act of 1939,which embeds the UAC in publicly issued corporate bond contracts in the United States,therefore implying that a path dependency constrains the drafting of New York sovereign contracts. We reject this contract failure explanation and propose instead a multiple equilibrium explanation. Under this explanation, UACs and CACs are both rational solutions to an intractable problem. The choice between the two entails trade offs, and is a matter of lender preference under uncertainty rather than a function of an efficiency calculation. One factor leading lenders to favor UACs is the lack of a good faith backstop, which results in a need for self-protection. Holding out is the only weapon one has in aworld in which creditors motivated by side deals can impose suboptimal compositions by majority rule.
Part V projects that such side deals and giveaways will occur if sovereign debt compositions are negotiated under CACs. Resolution of these disputes, therefore, requires a robust good faith principle. We draw on the history of corporate reorganization prior to the enactment of section 77B of the Bankruptcy Act of 1934to show that courts have grappled with these questions before, intervening on equitable principles.

matches.theme_name: Do collective-action clauses (CACs), unanimity clauses (UACs), and related contractual devices reliably prevent holdouts and enable orderly sovereign debt restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article contends that unanimity clauses (UACs) impede restructurings and invite holdouts, while collective-action clauses (CACs) ease coordination but, without an enforceable intercreditor good-faith backstop, permit opportunistic side deals that can undermine orderly workouts.
matches.generalized_contribution: Unanimity requirements exacerbate holdouts, whereas majority-action provisions facilitate coordination but do not reliably deliver orderly restructurings absent enforceable intercreditor good-faith constraints.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal bargaining model of sovereign debt restructuring that characterizes when creditors prefer UACs over CACs given the risk of opportunistic side deals and the presence or absence of enforceable intercreditor good-faith duties.

matches.theme_name: Which institutional or doctrinal reforms (statutory sovereign bankruptcy, coordinated creditor fora, harmonized conflict-of-laws rules) are feasible and likely to improve restructuring speed, predictability, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article argues that a voluntary market-wide shift from UACs to CACs is unlikely and, even in a best case, would require mandatory intervention or penalties, and proposes a minimal statutory regime that overrides UACs with CACs, limits IMF administrative involvement, and supplies adjudicatory enforcement of intercreditor good-faith duties to improve restructuring outcomes.
matches.generalized_contribution: A minimal statutory framework that mandates majority action and enforces intercreditor good faith is more feasible and likely to enhance restructuring speed and fairness than relying on spontaneous contract change or expansive IMF administration.
matches.research_idea: Design and analytically evaluate a minimal statutory sovereign restructuring regime that voids unanimity voting on payment terms and institutes judicially enforceable intercreditor good-faith duties, comparing its feasibility and predicted outcomes to a contract-only transition and to an IMF-administered system.

matches.theme_name: Can contractual devices (collateral, covenants, exit consents, priority clauses) effectively allocate and limit creditor risk in sovereign and cross-border transactions under information asymmetry?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article explains that, absent enforceable intercreditor good-faith duties, creditors may rationally favor UACs as self-protection against opportunistic majority amendments and side deals that CACs can enable.
matches.generalized_contribution: Where intercreditor protections are weak, unanimity provisions can function as a rational risk-allocation device against opportunistic restructuring tactics.
matches.research_idea: Analyze how the existence or absence of enforceable intercreditor good-faith obligations shifts creditors’ preferences between unanimity and majority-amendment clauses as risk-allocation mechanisms in sovereign debt contracts.

matches.theme_name: Do fragmented or indeterminate cross-border legal regimes create enforcement gaps that justify doctrinal or institutional reform for sovereign debt?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article identifies a doctrinal gap under New York law—undeveloped intercreditor good-faith duties in sovereign debt—that would permit opportunism under CACs and argues that a viable restructuring framework requires an adjudicatory authority to impose such duties, drawing on pre-1934 corporate reorganization equity for guidance.
matches.generalized_contribution: Indeterminate intercreditor-duty law in key governing jurisdictions creates enforcement gaps in sovereign restructurings that warrant coordinated reform to supply a good-faith backstop.
matches.research_idea: Characterize, using doctrinal analysis and historical comparison to pre-1934 corporate reorganizations, a framework for adjudicatory enforcement of intercreditor good-faith duties among sovereign creditors under New York law to close enforcement gaps in cross-border restructurings.

matches.theme_name: Are market-based restructuring instruments (debt-equity swaps, exit consents, buybacks) as effective and equitable as formal legal remedies in reallocating burdens during sovereign restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: Contrasting a contractarian path (market-led adoption of CACs) with a statutory sovereign bankruptcy approach, the Article concludes that market mechanisms alone are unlikely to yield effective restructurings and that a minimal legal regime mandating majority action and policing intercreditor opportunism is preferable to both pure contract solutions and an administratively heavy IMF system.
matches.generalized_contribution: Market-only approaches to sovereign restructuring are insufficient; a formal legal framework that mandates majority action and curbs intercreditor opportunism is more effective and equitable than voluntary mechanisms alone.
matches.research_idea: Compare, within a formal bargaining framework, the effectiveness and distributive properties of a voluntary CAC-based restructuring process versus a minimal statutory regime that imposes CACs and intercreditor good-faith duties.

matches.theme_name: How do domestic courts, international arbitration, and official institutions (e.g., IMF) interact to determine bargaining leverage and the legality of restructuring plans?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a theoretical analysis of sovereign lending and restructuring, the article explains that IMF bailouts erode creditors’ incentives to concede, IMF administrative involvement in an SDRM adds little value, and once UACs are replaced by CACs, bargaining leverage and legality should instead be grounded in New York courts’ imposition of intercreditor good‑faith duties.
matches.generalized_contribution: Official bailout policies shift bargaining leverage, while legality and coordination in restructurings are better anchored in domestic court enforcement of intercreditor good‑faith duties than in multilateral administrative control.
matches.research_idea: Analyze how IMF bailout policy and a New York–law, court‑centered regime interact to shape debtor and creditor bargaining leverage, modeling the effects of judicially imposed intercreditor good‑faith duties on restructuring outcomes.

matches.theme_name: Should courts defer to non-judicial determinations (trustee votes, arbitral panels, exchange mechanics) as dispositive in enforcing collective restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: The article contends that an effective restructuring framework requires an adjudicatory authority to impose intercreditor good‑faith duties and that IMF administrative involvement adds little, implying courts should not simply defer to non‑judicial exchange mechanics or administrators.
matches.generalized_contribution: Judicial oversight to police intercreditor opportunism is necessary for enforcing collective restructurings, rather than deference to private or multilateral administrative determinations.
matches.research_idea: Analyze the institutional tradeoffs of court‑centered oversight that imposes intercreditor good‑faith duties versus deference to trustee votes or IMF‑administered exchange mechanics in enforcing collective restructurings.

matches.theme_name: Are negotiated, policy-oriented processes through multilateral institutions more effective than formal international-law doctrines in resolving sovereign debt crises?
matches.specific_contribution: The article argues that IMF administrative involvement in a sovereign bankruptcy system lacks persuasive normative grounding and adds little value, favoring a minimalist approach that relies on CACs and domestic contract law with judicial good‑faith oversight.
matches.generalized_contribution: Negotiated IMF‑centered processes are not inherently more effective than minimalist, contract‑law‑based frameworks with judicial oversight.
matches.research_idea: Conduct a comparative institutional analysis of IMF‑led negotiated restructuring processes versus a minimalist CAC‑based regime enforced under domestic contract law, evaluating efficiency, legitimacy, and creditor welfare.

matches.theme_name: Would instituting a treaty/statutory Sovereign Debt Restructuring Mechanism (SDRM) reduce holdout litigation and crisis costs compared with reliance on ad-hoc private mechanisms?
matches.specific_contribution: The article argues that markets are unlikely to shift voluntarily from UACs to CACs, so reducing holdouts may require mandatory intervention to replace unanimity with majority action, but that any SDRM should be minimalist and paired with judicial enforcement of intercreditor good‑faith duties rather than heavy administrative control.
matches.generalized_contribution: A statutory mechanism mandating majority action can curb holdouts when markets will not self‑adopt CACs, but it should be minimalist and coupled with judicial policing of intercreditor opportunism.
matches.research_idea: Characterize the conditions under which a minimalist statutory mechanism that replaces unanimity with majority action reduces holdout costs, and analyze the role of judicially enforced intercreditor duties in such a regime.

matches.theme_name: Are out-of-court exchange offers and market-based restructuring techniques as effective as formal insolvency analogues in securing broad creditor cooperation?
matches.specific_contribution: The article suggests that with CACs in place and courts willing to impose intercreditor good‑faith duties, restructurings can proceed without a full bankruptcy infrastructure, though side deals under CACs necessitate judicial oversight.
matches.generalized_contribution: CAC‑based out‑of‑court restructurings can substitute for formal insolvency processes if accompanied by robust judicial policing of intercreditor conduct.
matches.research_idea: Analyze the comparative effectiveness of CAC‑based exchange offers supplemented by court‑enforced intercreditor duties versus formal insolvency‑style mechanisms in achieving broad creditor cooperation.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do holdout creditors (activist/vulture funds) influence restructuring terms, litigation patterns, and sovereign fiscal outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that under UACs, holdout behavior is a rational self‑protection strategy in the absence of a good‑faith backstop, while under CACs side deals and giveaways can let majorities impose suboptimal compositions, showing minority tactics materially shape restructuring terms.
matches.generalized_contribution: Holdout and opportunistic creditor behavior materially influence restructuring outcomes when unanimity rules or weak intercreditor duties permit leverage or side deals.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model of creditor bargaining under UACs versus CACs with and without judicially enforced good‑faith duties to characterize when holdouts emerge and how they affect restructuring terms.

matches.theme_name: Can clearer, mandatory contractual defaults (e.g., standard voting rules, enforcement waivers) improve predictability without producing adverse distributional or moral-hazard effects?
matches.specific_contribution: Using a conceptual analysis of sovereign lending and amendment clauses, the Article contends that a market-wide shift from UACs to CACs will not occur voluntarily and should be mandated only within a minimal regime that replaces unanimity with majority action and adds an adjudicatory intercreditor good-faith duty to curb opportunism and preserve predictability.
matches.generalized_contribution: Mandatory, standardized majority-amendment defaults can enhance restructurability and predictability only if coupled with enforceable intercreditor good-faith constraints; voluntary adoption risks stagnation and opportunism.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model comparing unanimity and majority-amendment defaults to characterize when mandating CACs alongside judicially enforced intercreditor good-faith duties improves predictability without inducing moral hazard or adverse distributional effects.

matches.theme_name: How do market conditions and relative bargaining power among actors determine debt terms, restructuring allocations, and recovery outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article explains that IMF bailout prospects and tripartite bargaining among sovereigns, creditors, and the IMF alter incentives by weakening creditors’ willingness to concede, complicating restructuring dynamics independent of clause design.
matches.generalized_contribution: Anticipated official-sector support and multiparty bargaining dynamics can dampen creditors’ negotiation incentives and shape restructuring outcomes regardless of contract terms.
matches.research_idea: Analyze within a theoretical tripartite negotiation framework how the prospect of IMF lending shifts bargaining power and concession patterns in sovereign debt restructurings.

matches.theme_name: Do the legal norms and contracting practices centered in major financial hubs (New York, London) produce convergence in sovereign-debt contract terms worldwide, and under what mechanisms?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article rejects a Trust Indenture Act path-dependence account of New York UACs versus London CACs and advances a multiple-equilibria explanation in which both clause types are rational given legal backstops (including the absence of intercreditor good-faith duties) and creditor preferences under uncertainty.
matches.generalized_contribution: Divergent sovereign-debt terms across New York and London can persist due to multiple equilibria shaped by legal context and creditor preferences, rather than converging through hub dominance.
matches.research_idea: Develop a model of clause selection under differing legal backstops to identify conditions under which multiple equilibria sustain long-run divergence between New York and London amendment practices.

matches.theme_name: How does the composition and heterogeneity of creditors (official vs private, concentrated vs dispersed, activist vs passive) affect bargaining dynamics and distributional outcomes in restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article argues that heterogeneity and conflicting interests among creditor groups—manifesting under CAC-based restructurings through side deals and giveaways—require an adjudicatory authority to impose intercreditor good-faith duties to secure equitable outcomes.
matches.generalized_contribution: Creditor heterogeneity can generate opportunistic side deals in majority-driven restructurings, necessitating enforceable intercreditor duties to stabilize bargaining and distributions.
matches.research_idea: Develop a theoretical framework showing how intercreditor conflicts under majority voting affect bargaining and recoveries, and assess how imposing good-faith duties changes equilibrium outcomes.

matches.theme_name: Do majority amendment/exit-consent designs create adverse distributional effects for small or domestic creditors and taxpayers, and how should those trade-offs be governed?
matches.specific_contribution: Projecting that CAC-driven restructurings will feature side deals and giveaways that disadvantage subsets of creditors, the Article contends that these distributional concerns should be governed by a robust, adjudicated intercreditor good-faith principle.
matches.generalized_contribution: Majority-binding amendment mechanisms can impose adverse distributional effects on minority creditors unless constrained by enforceable good-faith norms.
matches.research_idea: Analyze, in a formal model of majority amendment, how good-faith constraints modify the distributional impact on minority creditors relative to an unconstrained CAC regime.

matches.theme_name: How does heterogeneity in creditor rights and intercreditor priority influence restructuring feasibility, bargaining dynamics, and recoveries?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article cautions that once renegotiation begins, some creditor groups may pursue side deals at others’ expense, showing how intra-creditor differences—rather than debtor behavior—can impede feasibility absent enforceable duties.
matches.generalized_contribution: Differences across creditor groups can undermine restructuring feasibility through intra-creditor opportunism unless bounded by shared obligations.
matches.research_idea: Model the feasibility of sovereign debt compositions when creditor groups differ in incentives, and analyze how intercreditor obligations affect the likelihood of agreement.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries, disclosure practices, and creditor composition (activist vs passive, domestic vs foreign) affect bargaining, pricing, and restructuring trajectories?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article notes that sovereign compositions are hindered by information asymmetries and coordination problems among dispersed bondholders, which interact with voting clauses to delay or derail agreements.
matches.generalized_contribution: Information asymmetries and investor dispersion amplify coordination failures in sovereign restructurings, especially under unanimity requirements.
matches.research_idea: Characterize in a theoretical bargaining model how information asymmetries and holder dispersion affect the likelihood and timing of successful restructuring under unanimity versus majority voting rules.

matches.theme_name: To what degree can contractual amendment mechanisms (exit consents, amendment clauses, consent thresholds) bind non-consenting creditors, and what are the legal and practical limits?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article maintains that while CACs can bind non-consenting creditors to amendments, their effectiveness is limited by the risk of opportunistic side deals and suboptimal compositions unless courts enforce intercreditor good-faith duties; accordingly, a minimal regime should replace UACs with CACs and rely on governing law to police creditor behavior.
matches.generalized_contribution: Majority-amendment clauses can bind holdouts but require judicially enforceable good-faith limits to prevent abuse and enable workable restructurings.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal analysis of majority amendment’s capacity to bind non-consenting creditors and delineate legal and practical limits with and without enforceable intercreditor good-faith obligations.

matches.theme_name: Which technical design features of amendment/exit-consent clauses (quorum thresholds, aggregation rules, consent solicitation) most effectively deter holdouts while maintaining market confidence?
matches.specific_contribution: Analyzing UACs versus CACs in sovereign bonds, the article argues that even absent IMF bailouts creditors may rationally prefer unanimous-consent regimes because majority-amendment CACs, without an enforceable intercreditor good-faith backstop, invite side deals and suboptimal compositions despite their holdout-deterrence benefits.
matches.generalized_contribution: Majority-amendment designs deter holdouts but can erode investor protection and confidence unless paired with enforceable intercreditor good-faith constraints, making UACs and CACs alternative rational equilibria rather than a simple efficiency ranking.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model comparing UAC and CAC regimes that incorporates the risk of side deals and the presence or absence of enforceable intercreditor good-faith duties, and characterize the parameter regions in which creditors prefer each design.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do legal ambiguities and doctrinal vagueness (e.g., in 'pari passu', 'loan' definitions, or damages measures) cause litigation, market uncertainty, and suboptimal contracting outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: Grounded in New York sovereign debt practice, the article highlights that the law is undeveloped on whether creditors owe one another good-faith duties, and contends that this doctrinal gap fosters opportunistic side deals and disputes in majority-amendment restructurings.
matches.generalized_contribution: Doctrinal uncertainty about intercreditor good-faith obligations increases opportunism and dispute risk in sovereign debt restructurings.
matches.research_idea: Analyze how uncertainty over intercreditor good-faith duties under New York law shapes opportunistic behavior in sovereign restructurings, and derive a workable good-faith standard by synthesizing pre-1934 equitable reorganization precedents.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do standardized boilerplate clauses (e.g., pari passu, governing-law, indemnities) generate systemic litigation externalities and market-wide vulnerabilities?
matches.specific_contribution: Focusing on boilerplate amendment clauses in sovereign bonds, the article argues that entrenched use of UACs creates systemic coordination and holdout vulnerabilities, while a broad shift to CACs without a good-faith backstop would introduce correlated risks of side deals and suboptimal outcomes, making spontaneous market transition unlikely without mandates or subsidies.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized amendment boilerplate can propagate market-wide vulnerabilities—holdout risk under unanimity clauses and abuse risk under majority clauses absent good-faith constraints—producing correlated restructuring failures unless external discipline or incentives are added.
matches.research_idea: Characterize market-wide equilibria generated by widespread use of UACs versus CACs—with and without enforceable intercreditor good-faith duties—using a multiple-equilibria framework informed by New York- and London-law contracting practice.

matches.theme_name: Can private ordering, market-level contractual design, and intermediaries substitute effectively for statutory or multilateral interventions in solving cross-border collective-action problems?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article argues that a voluntary, market-led shift from unanimous action clauses (UACs) to collective action clauses (CACs) is unlikely because lenders can rationally prefer UACs and, absent intercreditor good-faith duties, multiple equilibria and side-deal risks impede coordination—implying that mandatory intervention or aggressive official-sector pressure would be needed to achieve majority-action restructuring.
matches.generalized_contribution: Private ordering alone cannot reliably solve sovereign restructuring collective-action problems; without intercreditor protections, markets may remain stuck on unanimity terms, necessitating mandatory or official-sector solutions.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model comparing UACs and CACs in a setting without enforceable intercreditor good-faith duties to characterize when voluntary contract evolution fails and when mandatory CACs or official-sector inducements are required to achieve coordination.

matches.theme_name: What institutional reforms of the IMF and other multilateral actors would improve coordination of sovereign restructurings without creating undue moral hazard?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article contends that the IMF’s proposed administrative role in a sovereign bankruptcy architecture adds little and may conflict with creditors’ best interests, advocating instead a minimal regime that installs CACs and relies on creditor approval, with any IMF involvement limited to using conditionality to pressure contract standardization rather than administering cases.
matches.generalized_contribution: Expansive IMF administrative reforms are unnecessary; a minimal framework centered on creditor consent with at most targeted conditionality can enhance coordination without amplifying moral hazard.
matches.research_idea: Analyze, within a comparative institutional framework, whether a minimal CAC-trumping regime grounded in creditor approval outperforms an IMF-administered restructuring mechanism on coordination efficacy and moral hazard.

matches.theme_name: Should international financial institutions (IMF/World Bank) be given expanded mandates (stays, priority lending, formal restructuring roles) to manage sovereign-debt crises, and what are the trade-offs?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article argues against granting the IMF a broad formal restructuring mandate, proposing instead a minimal intervention that simply overrides UACs with CACs and defers to creditor consent, with any IMF role confined to pressuring adoption of model terms rather than administering restructurings.
matches.generalized_contribution: Expanded official-sector authority over restructurings is unwarranted; limited interventions to enable majority action while preserving creditor decision-making suffice.
matches.research_idea: Characterize the trade-offs of empowering international financial institutions with case-administration powers versus limiting them to inducing CAC adoption, using a formal institutional design analysis.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries, hidden actors, and disclosure regimes shape bargaining dynamics, pricing, and the incidence of holdouts in restructurings?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article notes that information asymmetries and coordination problems impede compositions and that, under CACs, opaque side deals among creditor factions can yield suboptimal majority-imposed outcomes absent enforceable good-faith duties.
matches.generalized_contribution: Incomplete information and hidden side arrangements among creditors can distort bargaining and exacerbate coordination failures in restructurings without intercreditor constraints.
matches.research_idea: Develop a bargaining model of sovereign restructuring with dispersed creditors to examine how undisclosed side deals under majority-action clauses affect holdout incentives and the efficiency of negotiated outcomes.

matches.theme_name: What are the welfare trade-offs of prioritizing orderly, negotiated restructuring (stability and debtor rehabilitation) over strict creditor protections?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article maintains that although CACs can facilitate orderly restructurings, regimes should be governed by a creditors’ best-interest norm that permits deals to fail and guards against coercive majority compositions, underscoring the trade-off between stability and strict creditor protections.
matches.generalized_contribution: Policies favoring orderly restructurings should be constrained by creditor-consent standards to prevent efficiency-seeking bargains from undermining creditor welfare.
matches.research_idea: Develop an analytical framework comparing welfare under unanimity versus majority-action clauses when coercive or side-deal dynamics may arise, identifying conditions under which orderly restructuring improves or harms creditor welfare.

matches.theme_name: What role do the IMF and other official-sector actors play in shaping restructuring bargaining, creditor incentives, and ultimate debt-relief outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: The article explains that IMF bailout practices and official-sector pressure shape restructuring by dulling creditors’ incentives to negotiate concessions, prompting selective CAC adoption, and that the IMF’s proposed administrative role in a sovereign bankruptcy mechanism adds little value relative to a minimalist regime that simply replaces UACs with CACs and relies on contract law.
matches.generalized_contribution: Official-sector financing and institutional design choices materially alter creditor coordination and bargaining leverage, and a minimalist majority-action framework can substitute for IMF-administered restructuring without sacrificing creditor interests.
matches.research_idea: Analyze how expected bailouts, official-sector pressure, and alternative administrative designs affect sovereign–creditor bargaining using a formal model with a sovereign, dispersed creditors, and an IMF-like actor.

matches.theme_name: Should courts or legislators prioritize textual formalism or pragmatic crisis-management when resolving disputes implicating sovereign obligations?
matches.specific_contribution: The article argues for a minimalist legal intervention—overriding UACs with CACs while eschewing deal-closing pragmatism—and for courts to enforce intercreditor good-faith duties under governing contract law rather than manage restructurings to completion.
matches.generalized_contribution: In sovereign debt disputes, prioritizing contract-based creditor consent and judicially enforced intercreditor duties over crisis-driven efforts to force agreements better aligns with long-run creditor and sovereign interests.
matches.research_idea: Develop a normative and formal analysis comparing outcomes under a minimalist majority-action regime with judicial good-faith policing to those under a crisis-management regime that prioritizes swift deal closure.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do choice-of-law and forum-selection clauses determine the enforceability of claims against sovereigns?
matches.specific_contribution: By noting that most bonds are governed by New York law—which lacks developed intercreditor good-faith duties—and observing the persistent split between New York-based UACs and London-based CACs, the article links governing law to both renegotiation dynamics and clause choice.
matches.generalized_contribution: Governing-law choices that supply or withhold intercreditor duties influence both the feasibility of enforcing claims in restructuring and the market’s selection of amendment mechanisms.
matches.research_idea: Analyze how the presence or absence of intercreditor good-faith duties under different governing laws shifts renegotiation outcomes and the relative attractiveness of unanimous- versus collective-action amendment clauses within a formal framework.

matches.theme_name: Do problems of information asymmetry versus Knightian uncertainty lead to different contractual designs and renegotiation dynamics in distressed transactions?
matches.specific_contribution: The article distinguishes practical barriers from information asymmetries and shows that, under uncertainty about restructuring outcomes and without a good-faith backstop, lenders may rationally prefer UACs to CACs despite coordination costs.
matches.generalized_contribution: Deep uncertainty and the availability of governance backstops, not just information asymmetry, can push contracting parties toward more veto-heavy amendment rules in distressed settings.
matches.research_idea: Characterize the equilibrium choice between unanimous and collective amendment rules by separating the effects of information asymmetry from model uncertainty and intercreditor opportunism in a formal bargaining model.

matches.theme_name: How do market conditions, bargaining power, and counterparty composition drive adoption and specific wording of non-price clauses (MAE/MAC, covenants, break fees) in M&A and lending contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: Proposing a multiple-equilibria account, the article contends that the long-standing split between UACs and CACs reflects lender preferences under uncertainty and the absence of intercreditor good-faith protections, with official-sector bailouts and pressure further shifting adoption dynamics.
matches.generalized_contribution: Adoption of non-price amendment clauses is jointly driven by market beliefs, creditor composition, and public-sector interventions, producing persistent clause heterogeneity even without clear efficiency dominance.
matches.research_idea: Develop a multiple-equilibria model in which creditor heterogeneity, expectations about official-sector support, and legal backstops determine the adoption and persistence of alternative amendment clauses.

matches.theme_name: How effective are international financial institutions (IMF/Bretton Woods) and official-sector actors in shaping restructuring incentives and practical outcomes relative to private creditors?
matches.specific_contribution: The article contends that IMF bailouts often weaken creditors' incentives to negotiate concessions, that IMF administrative involvement in a sovereign bankruptcy framework would add little value, and that a broad shift from UACs to CACs will likely require mandatory official-sector pressure or costly inducements rather than spontaneous market action.
matches.generalized_contribution: Official-sector actions can both distort bargaining incentives through bailouts and be necessary to shift contract terms, while administrative oversight by international financial institutions is not inherently value-adding to restructuring outcomes.
matches.research_idea: Develop a theoretical framework comparing private ordering and official-sector interventions in sovereign restructurings to characterize when bailouts, penalty threats, or mandates shift clause adoption and improve bargaining incentives, and when administrative involvement is redundant.

matches.theme_name: Why do standardized contractual clauses ('boilerplate') persist despite inefficiencies, and what institutional or market mechanisms overcome this lock-in?
matches.specific_contribution: Rejecting path-dependence accounts tied to the Trust Indenture Act, the article explains the century-long persistence of UACs in New York-law sovereign bonds as a multiple-equilibrium outcome sustained by rational lender preferences and the absence of intercreditor good-faith duties, implying that transition to CACs will stall without subsidies or mandates.
matches.generalized_contribution: Boilerplate can persist because multiple rational equilibria exist under uncertainty and weak governance, and moving to alternative terms may require affirmative incentives or regulation rather than spontaneous market correction.
matches.research_idea: Develop a multiple-equilibrium model of sovereign bond amendment clauses that incorporates uncertainty and missing intercreditor good-faith enforcement, and derive conditions under which market forces versus regulatory mandates overcome entrenched UAC usage.

matches.theme_name: How do information asymmetries-adverse selection and moral hazard-shape the design of contractual devices (collateral, covenants, disclosure) in sovereign and corporate lending?
matches.specific_contribution: In motivating the need for effective amendment mechanisms, the article notes that information asymmetries are among the practical barriers that complicate sovereign debt compositions alongside coordination and bargaining frictions.
matches.generalized_contribution: Information asymmetries can hinder sovereign debt renegotiations, amplifying coordination problems that contract design must address.
matches.research_idea: Analyze how information asymmetries interact with coordination frictions to affect restructuring feasibility under UACs versus CACs using a formal bargaining model.

matches.theme_name: When do private ordering and standardized boilerplate generate negative externalities for third parties that warrant public-policy or regulatory intervention?
matches.specific_contribution: Using the century-long persistence of unanimous action clauses (UACs) in New York–law sovereign bonds and the limited, pressure-induced uptake of collective action clauses (CACs), the Article argues that private ordering can entrench coordination failures and intercreditor opportunism such that markets will not voluntarily transition to more efficient terms, implying the need for mandatory CACs or subsidies plus an adjudicatory good-faith backstop among creditors.
matches.generalized_contribution: When standardized boilerplate entrenches coordination failures and intercreditor opportunism, voluntary private ordering is unlikely to self-correct, warranting targeted mandatory rules and adjudication to protect broader systemic interests.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model of sovereign debt amendment clauses in which lender preferences and intercreditor opportunism create multiple equilibria, and characterize when voluntary transitions fail and when targeted mandates or subsidies plus good-faith duties improve welfare.

matches.theme_name: How do cross-border legal conflicts-choice-of-law, extraterritorial reach, and conflicting forum judgments-shape enforceability and predictability in international financial contracts?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article highlights the New York-versus-London split (UACs versus CACs) and rejects a path-dependence explanation tied to the U.S. Trust Indenture Act, proposing instead that both clause types can be rational equilibria driven by lender preferences rather than cross-border legal constraints.
matches.generalized_contribution: Differences in governing-law regimes need not deterministically shape contract design when multiple rational equilibria, sustained by investor preferences, allow divergent boilerplate across markets.
matches.research_idea: Analyze how New York and English governing-law environments interact with investor preferences in a coordination model to yield multiple equilibria in amendment-clause design and predict when shifts between UACs and CACs occur.

matches.theme_name: Do dispute-resolution architectures that shift authority to international fora create unintended incentive distortions or enforcement gaps?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article contends that an IMF-administered sovereign bankruptcy architecture adds little value and can distort bargaining by encouraging creditor passivity through bailout expectations, and favors a minimal intervention that simply overrides UACs with CACs and remits disputes to New York contract law, supplemented by intercreditor good-faith duties.
matches.generalized_contribution: Shifting restructuring authority to international fora can create perverse bargaining incentives, whereas minimal interventions enabling majority action and relying on domestic contract law may better align outcomes with creditor welfare.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model comparing bargaining and welfare under an IMF-run restructuring forum versus a minimal CAC-enabling regime governed by domestic law, and characterize how bailout expectations and administrative control affect creditor concessions and composition quality.

matches.theme_name: What role do lawyers, underwriters, and other intermediaries play in creating, diffusing, and entrenching contractual innovations and standard clauses?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article notes that elite law firms’ boilerplate amendment clauses have remained largely unchanged for a century and that recent moves toward CACs required official-sector pressure, while emphasizing that persistence reflects rational lender preferences more than drafting inertia.
matches.generalized_contribution: Intermediary-maintained boilerplate can persist due to market preferences rather than mere template inertia, and policy nudges may be necessary to dislodge entrenched terms.
matches.research_idea: Develop a multiple-equilibria model of clause adoption that incorporates law-firm templates, underwriter practices, and official-sector signals to determine when intermediaries can shift markets from UACs to CACs.

matches.theme_name: To what extent do information asymmetries and signaling affect creditor decision-making and pricing in sovereign and complex financial contracting?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article identifies information asymmetries, alongside coordination problems and complex bargaining dynamics, as practical barriers that impede sovereign debt compositions under dispersed bondholding and boilerplate amendment clauses.
matches.generalized_contribution: Information asymmetries hinder creditor coordination in sovereign restructurings, reinforcing holdout risks under standard amendment clauses.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model of sovereign debt restructuring in which creditor information asymmetries and bailout expectations jointly determine holdout incentives and the choice between unanimity and majority-action clauses.

matches.theme_name: Does the extraterritorial reach of national legal regimes and conflicting jurisdictional claims produce distortive conflicts-of-law that affect capital flows and contract design?
matches.specific_contribution: By noting that most sovereign bonds are governed by New York law, where intercreditor good-faith duties are undeveloped, the Article explains why creditors may rationally prefer UACs as self-protection against opportunistic majority action, and rejects a simple path-dependence account tied to the Trust Indenture Act.
matches.generalized_contribution: Differences in governing-law doctrines on intercreditor duties can shape creditor preferences for unanimity versus majority-action clauses in cross-border sovereign bonds.
matches.research_idea: Analyze, within a comparative doctrinal and analytical framework, how the presence or absence of intercreditor good-faith duties under competing governing laws (e.g., New York versus English law) shifts equilibrium demand for collective-action versus unanimity clauses.

matches.theme_name: Would greater doctrinal clarity (narrowed exceptions, precise rules) improve predictability enough to sustain cross-border lending and reduce costly strategic behavior?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article argues that resolving opportunism and side deals under CAC-based restructurings requires an adjudicatory authority to impose robust intercreditor good-faith duties, given New York law’s underdevelopment on such duties.
matches.generalized_contribution: Clarifying and enforcing intercreditor good-faith duties would improve predictability and curb opportunism in majority-action sovereign restructurings.
matches.research_idea: Characterize the conditions under which a robust intercreditor good-faith standard deters opportunistic side deals in majority-vote sovereign restructurings using a formal bargaining framework.

matches.theme_name: How do legal and institutional shocks (financial crises, regime change, pandemics) drive changes in contractual practice and market pricing?
matches.specific_contribution: Using the post-Argentina shift away from automatic IMF bailouts and limited official-sector pressure as context, the Article projects that a market-wide transition from UACs to CACs will not occur spontaneously because rational lender preferences and frictions impede change, absent subsidies or mandates.
matches.generalized_contribution: Crisis- or policy-driven shocks alone do not reliably induce adoption of pro-restructuring contract terms without added incentives or coercive intervention.
matches.research_idea: Develop a model of contract-term diffusion in sovereign bond markets that specifies when official-sector policy shifts and crisis episodes overcome coordination frictions and creditor preferences to trigger transitions from unanimity to majority-action clauses.

matches.theme_name: Does statutory codification of contractual standards produce faster or qualitatively different change in drafting practice than incremental common-law evolution?
matches.specific_contribution: The Article concludes that because lenders may rationally prefer UACs and frictions block voluntary change, achieving a majority-action regime likely requires mandatory intervention—such as IMF-imposed model terms backed by penalties—rather than relying on spontaneous market evolution.
matches.generalized_contribution: Statutory or regulatory imposition of contractual standards can be necessary to effect broad, rapid change in boilerplate when market incentives entrench the status quo.
matches.research_idea: Analyze how mandatory codification of collective-action clauses, versus reliance on incremental market evolution, affects equilibrium contract terms in a model with heterogeneous creditor preferences and coordination costs.

matches.theme_name: When and to what extent should courts reinterpret or override standardized contract language to achieve equitable outcomes without sacrificing contractual certainty?
matches.specific_contribution: In the setting of sovereign bond restructurings largely governed by New York law, the article advocates minimally overriding unanimous-action boilerplate with collective-action terms and equipping an adjudicator to impose intercreditor good-faith duties to curb opportunistic side deals while preserving contractual governance.
matches.generalized_contribution: Targeted overrides of boilerplate coupled with enforceable intercreditor good-faith duties can deliver equitable restructuring outcomes without sacrificing contractual certainty.
matches.research_idea: Characterize the doctrinal thresholds under New York contract law for imposing intercreditor good-faith duties and justify minimal statutory substitution of CACs for UACs to prevent opportunism in sovereign restructurings.

matches.theme_name: How does judicial interpretive flexibility (vague standards vs precise rules) affect predictability and market behavior in high-stakes transactional and sovereign debt litigation?
matches.specific_contribution: Because New York law lacks a clear intercreditor good-faith standard, creditors rationally favor rigid unanimity clauses; thus any shift to majority-rule CACs must be paired with a robust, adjudicated good-faith standard to manage opportunism and preserve credible restructuring governance.
matches.generalized_contribution: Judicially enforceable good-faith standards enable flexible majority-action mechanisms, while their absence pushes markets toward rigid rules for self-protection and predictability.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model comparing outcomes under unanimity (rule-like) versus majority-action (standard-based) clauses, with and without an adjudicated intercreditor good-faith duty, to assess effects on predictability and holdout behavior in sovereign debt.

matches.theme_name: What are the trade-offs between standardized boilerplate and bespoke drafting for transaction costs, liquidity, and fairness?
matches.specific_contribution: Using the contrast between New York- and London-governed sovereign bonds, the article advances a multiple-equilibria account in which both UAC and CAC boilerplate are rational choices, with lenders potentially preferring UACs in the absence of a good-faith backstop against opportunistic majority deals.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized boilerplate choices reflect rational trade-offs under uncertainty, with parties selecting unanimity or majority-action terms based on intercreditor-opportunism risk and the availability of protective enforcement norms.
matches.research_idea: Characterize the conditions under which markets select UACs versus CACs as stable equilibria by modeling how intercreditor opportunism and enforceable good-faith duties shift efficiency and fairness trade-offs in standardized clauses.

matches.theme_name: Does diffusion of standardized contract clauses across jurisdictions reduce transaction costs and improve predictability for investors?
matches.specific_contribution: Appraising the CAC-versus-UAC debate across New York and London markets, the Article argues—via a multiple-equilibrium account—that lenders can rationally prefer UACs even absent IMF bailouts, so a market-wide diffusion to CACs will not spontaneously occur or lower restructuring frictions without payments or mandatory intervention.
matches.generalized_contribution: Diffusion of standardized majority-amendment clauses does not inherently reduce restructuring costs or increase predictability when competing boilerplate regimes reflect rational preferences and legal frictions.
matches.research_idea: Develop a multiple-equilibrium model of clause diffusion across jurisdictions to characterize when markets adopt CACs versus UACs and whether standardization reduces coordination and restructuring costs in the presence of official-sector pressure and legal backstops.

matches.theme_name: To what extent does legal indeterminacy and doctrinal vagueness increase transaction costs and reduce cross-border capital flows?
matches.specific_contribution: Identifying an underdeveloped New York jurisprudence on intercreditor good-faith duties and drawing on pre-1934 reorganization practice, the Article explains that legal gaps enable opportunistic side deals under CACs, push creditors toward unanimity rules as self-protection, and raise renegotiation and coordination costs unless an adjudicator imposes cross-creditor good-faith obligations.
matches.generalized_contribution: Legal indeterminacy about intercreditor duties increases renegotiation frictions and distorts clause selection toward unanimity mechanisms unless enforceable good-faith obligations constrain creditor opportunism.
matches.research_idea: Develop a formal model of sovereign debt restructuring with heterogeneous creditor groups to analyze how the presence or absence of enforceable intercreditor good-faith duties affects the relative efficiency of unanimity versus collective-action amendment rules and the resulting negotiation costs.

matches.theme_name: Do standardized contract forms and drafting defaults systematically shape non-price deal terms and bargaining outcomes?
matches.specific_contribution: Examining sovereign bond boilerplate, the Article shows that entrenched amendment defaults (UACs versus CACs) systematically shape restructuring bargaining—allocating holdout power and exposure to side deals—and that persistent reliance on UACs can be a rational lender choice in the absence of good-faith backstops, undermining assumptions that CACs are universally first-best.
matches.generalized_contribution: Standardized amendment defaults in debt contracts determine bargaining leverage and outcomes, with strong unanimity rules empowering holdouts when intercreditor protections are weak.
matches.research_idea: Analyze bargaining equilibria under unanimity and supermajority amendment defaults with opportunistic creditor types and varying good-faith enforcement to characterize how drafting defaults shape non-price outcomes in sovereign restructurings.

matches.theme_name: Do legal-opinion practices and interpretive uncertainty among advisors increase transaction costs and systematically shape how contracts are drafted and priced?
matches.specific_contribution: Using doctrinal analysis of New York law and historical corporate reorganization practice, the article argues that uncertainty and the absence of enforceable intercreditor good-faith duties induce creditors to favor unanimous action clauses over collective action clauses as a form of contractual self-protection.
matches.generalized_contribution: Interpretive uncertainty about intercreditor obligations under governing law drives parties toward veto-protective amendment mechanisms and away from coordination-facilitating terms.
matches.research_idea: Analyze how uncertainty about intercreditor good-faith obligations under governing law affects equilibrium clause choice between unanimous and collective action amendment provisions in sovereign bonds within a multiple-equilibria framework.

matches.theme_name: How do norms, professional networks, and market practice diffuse contractual innovations (like new clause language) across jurisdictions and market segments?
matches.specific_contribution: Comparing New York- and London-governed sovereign bond practices and recent issuer experiments with CACs, the article posits that UACs and CACs reflect multiple equilibria sustained by creditor preferences and self-protection norms, so broad diffusion of CACs will not occur spontaneously and will likely require side payments or mandatory/official-sector intervention.
matches.generalized_contribution: When clause choice reflects multiple equilibria grounded in creditor preferences and self-protection, contractual innovations like majority-action terms diffuse only with external incentives or mandates, allowing cross-jurisdictional divergence to persist.
matches.research_idea: Characterize the conditions under which a contractual innovation such as collective action clauses diffuses across jurisdictions in a coordination-game model with heterogeneous creditor preferences and an official-sector actor capable of imposing penalties or offering side payments.
